project_summary: A Drupal 11 upgrade for the Oklahoma Senate, with clearer typography, stronger accessibility and a production upgrade window under five minutes.
project_intro:
A government website has to keep working while the technology underneath it changes. For the Oklahoma Senate, our team upgraded a legacy Drupal platform, improved everyday usability and rehearsed the release until a complex deployment became a repeatable procedure.

My contribution: Drupal development, front-end accessibility and typography, release preparation and post-launch support, as part of a subcontracting team.

story_sections.story_html:
Keep the service. Renew the foundations.

The site was around six years old. Its platform and dependencies needed a substantial update, while senators, staff and the public still depended on its content and services. The brief was to reach Drupal 11 while preserving the familiar website and its content-management workflows.

That meant working through contributed-module compatibility, JavaScript dependencies and custom functionality, alongside the less visible work of making a production release predictable.

A familiar identity, a more readable website

I consolidated inconsistent typography, increased undersized text and improved text contrast across the existing interface. A Figma style reference collected the typography rules so that changes followed a shared visual language.

On smaller screens, I corrected wrapping, spacing, navigation and button alignment. Dense tables, senator pages and form controls received particular attention. The aim was practical: make the information easier to read and the controls easier to use while respecting the Senate’s established identity.

Accessibility improvements you can measure

The project notes record a Lighthouse accessibility score rising from 91 to 98 out of 100. Automated checks helped identify and validate improvements alongside page-by-page review. These results describe the release under test; later content changes can affect the score. They do not establish complete accessibility compliance.

What is Lighthouse? It is an automated website auditing tool available in Chrome DevTools, with separate checks for accessibility, performance and other aspects of page quality. To try it, open a page in Chrome, open DevTools, select Lighthouse and run an audit.

How to use Lighthouse in Chrome — Google’s guide

From a three-hour rehearsal to a release under five minutes

I prepared a pre-production environment where the production upgrade could be rehearsed and verified. The first run took roughly three hours while I worked through the commands and their responses.

Those rehearsals became a step-by-step release runbook with expected output, recovery guidance and a tested sequence. It made the procedure usable by another team member or system administrator if the original developer was unavailable.

By release, the production upgrade window was under five minutes, according to the engagement notes. The gain came from resolving uncertainty before the release: compatible dependencies, a known sequence and clear verification steps.

The engagement also established an accessible Git repository and a GitLab deployment workflow, with runtime content separated from application code.

Follow through on the details

Post-upgrade support included repairing video sharing from a chosen timestamp and resolving the homepage carousel’s compatibility with newer jQuery. I also traced broken layouts to malformed or escaped HTML in legacy content, using analysis of an approximately 2 GB database to find cases that were impractical to inspect manually.

When the site was reported to feel slower, the investigation separated application behaviour from hosting and the protective proxy layer. The engagement notes attribute the delay to that infrastructure layer rather than Drupal 11 itself. A media CDN was considered but not adopted because its cost offered limited value for a predominantly Oklahoma audience.

A stronger foundation for the next change

The result was a Drupal 11 website with improved readability, corrected mobile layouts and a documented release process. Just as valuable was the ability to repeat the work: shared typography rules, version-controlled code, a rehearsal environment and a runbook the team could follow.
